newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain conservatives promise further benefits ahead.
newsitem.headline: Spain conservatives promise further benefits ahead.

text.p: Spain's conservative government claimed credit on Friday for a sharp drop in inflation and thriving markets and promised more economic progress ahead.

"We have stopped being a country accustomed to relatively high inflation ... and this is the fruit of economic policies of liberalisation that we are applying and that we will continue to apply in 1997," Spanish Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro told Reuters in an interview.
The conservative Popular Party, which won a March election ending 13 years of Socialist rule, pushed through an austere budget for 1997 and liberalisation measures from savings to telecommunications.

The moves infused financial markets with confidence Spain would kick itself into shape for Europe's single currency launch in 1999 and helped prompt a sharp drop in inflation, long- and short-term interest rates as well as a firmer peseta.
"The Spanish state has entered 1997 breathing easier," Montoro said. "But we have by no means completed our task. We have to work everyday. There is no complacence in the Spanish government."

Montoro dismissed critics who have argued that huge gains in Spanish financial markets are overdone. They argue that markets have run ahead of themselves and are gaining ground on an over optimistic outlook.
They say the market's forecast for sharp improvement in inflation, the public deficit and interest rates may never fulfilled.
Spanish stocks soared in 1996 to become the year's top performer outside emerging markets.
The Madrid bourse rose nearly 40 percent and has continued to set new highs this year.

The benchmark bond has outpaced its more stolid German counterpart, with the yield differential sinking to its lowest levels ever at 89 basis points from 330 last March, in a reflection of the diminishing risk of holding Spanish issues over German.
"This isn't an overreaction. This is Spain adjusting to its current fundamentals," Montoro said.
There are further benefits ahead, Montoro added.
Consumer inflation will fall beneath three percent in the first quarter and the government will meet its 1997 price goal comfortably.
On Wednesday, Spain published data showing the inflation rate fell to 3.2 percent in December, beneath the government's mid-year target of 3.4 percent, and the lowest level in almost 30 years.

"The annual consumer price index growth rate is going to be below three percent in the first quarter of the year," Montoro said. "The 1997 objective is 2.6 percent, but just as in 1996, we could manage to achieve this objective comfortably."
He added that yields on shorter maturity paper should also decline and debt issuance will be reduced.

The difference between yields on Spanish and German two- and three-year paper are at some 200 basis points while at the long end, the spread between bonos and Bunds has dipped to about 90 points from 330 last March.
"As inflation moderates and there are visible and tough controls on the public deficit, the outlook for short-term rates is also downward," Montoro said.
"I understand this is the outlook on which the market is betting," he said.
